title: The Iron Girl and the Paper Dragon
summary: The town pays tribute to a fearsome dragon no one has ever seen up close. When Wren is chosen to be given to it, she goes armed and furious — and discovers that the most frightening monster in the world might be someone as lonely and scared as she is.

chapters.title: The Tribute
chapters.body:
The town of Highwall had lived in fear for so long that it had forgotten what it was like to live without it.

The fear had a name: Cinderscale, the Dragon of Smoke, who lived on the cracked mountain beyond the walls. No one alive had seen it up close — those who went near didn't come back — but everyone knew the signs. The black smoke that rose from the mountain when it was angry. The tremor in the earth when it moved. And, once a year, the roar: a terrible sound that came down the mountain and rattled the windows and made babies cry in their cradles.

When the roar came, the town knew what to do, because it had been doing it for a hundred years. It prepared the tribute. A cart full of gold, of food, of everything the town had that was best. And — this was the part no one liked to say aloud — a person. Chosen by lottery. To be given to the dragon along with the gold, because, the elders said, that was what kept it satisfied. That was what kept it from coming down and burning the whole town.

Wren was fourteen years old and believed none of it.

Not that she denied the dragon — the smoke was real, the roar was real. But she had questions no one could answer, and Wren was the sort of person whom unanswered questions made furious rather than afraid. How was it that no one had ever seen the dragon, yet everyone knew exactly what it wanted? How was it that it needed a person in particular, when dragons, from what she read in the old books, ate sheep and goats like any large beast? And why, if the tribute had worked for a hundred years, did the elders seem more frightened of the day of the lottery than of the dragon itself?

She was asking exactly those questions, loudly and to anyone who would listen in the square, on the day the roar came and the lottery was held. And — because life has a cruel sense of humor, or because someone behind the scenes found it convenient to silence the girl who asked too many questions — the name drawn was hers.

Wren.

Her grandmother wept. The whole town lowered its eyes, relieved it wasn't their turn, ashamed of their own relief. And the elders, with grave faces, said the usual words about sacrifice and the good of all.

But Wren did not weep. Wren went home, and instead of making peace with death, as was expected of her, she opened her grandfather's chest — he had been a soldier — and took out an old suit of leather and iron armor, small enough to fit her, and a short, well-sharpened dagger.

"If this dragon wants to eat me," she said to her grandmother, tightening the armor's straps with trembling but determined hands, "it's going to find out I'm a meal that bites back."

Her grandmother, through tears, held her face.

"No one comes back from the mountain, my love."

"Then I'll be the first," said Wren. "Or at least I'll be the first to make that lizard earn its dinner." But inside, despite all the fury, her heart beat like a trapped bird. Because courage, she was learning, is not the absence of fear. It is doing what must be done with the fear whole inside your chest.

chapters.title: The Cracked Mountain
chapters.body:
They took Wren to the foot of the mountain at dawn, with the tribute cart, and left her there. No one climbed with her. The guards unloaded the gold and the food at the entrance of the great cave from which the smoke came, avoided her eyes, and hurried away, almost running.

Wren stood alone before the dark mouth of the cave. The dagger in her hand. Her grandfather's armor tight on her body. The smell of sulfur and smoke in the air.

"ALL RIGHT, LIZARD!" she shouted into the dark, in the firmest voice her borrowed courage could muster. "I'M HERE! BUT I DIDN'T COME FOR FREE!"

Silence. And then, from the depths of the cave, a sound. Not the terrible roar. A far stranger sound: a rustling. A dry, light noise, like a thousand sheets of paper stirring at once.

Wren went in. The cave was enormous, dark, full of echoes, and the floor was covered in gold — a hundred years of tributes, mountains of coins and jewels untouched, dusty, as if no one had ever used them for anything. That was already strange. What does a dragon hoard gold for if it never spends it?

The rustling grew louder. Wren rounded a corner of stone, dagger forward, her heart in her throat, ready to face the monster.

And she stopped.

The Dragon of Smoke was there. It was enormous, yes — the size of a house, with wings that brushed the cave's ceiling, with claws and teeth and yellow eyes. But there was something terribly wrong with it. It was not made of scales. It was made of paper. Thousands upon thousands of sheets of paper — old, yellowed, covered in writing — folded and glued and layered into the shape of a dragon. A giant paper dragon, hollow, that moved with a dry rustle at each breath.

And inside it — Wren saw, when she got close enough, through a gap between the sheets of its chest — was a person.

A boy. Not much older than she was. Thin, pale, dirty, with deep circles under his eyes, sitting in the middle of a contraption of ropes and levers and bellows, inside the hollow chest of the paper dragon. He pulled the ropes and the dragon moved its claws. He blew into the bellows and the dragon's mouth let out the smoke. He shouted into a metal tube and the tube turned his voice into that terrible roar that made the town tremble.

The boy saw her see him. And the whole dragon froze, the rustling stopped, and for a long moment the two of them stared at each other — the iron girl with the dagger in her hand, and the paper boy hidden inside his own monster.

"You're not a dragon," said Wren, so astonished that all her fury evaporated. "You're a boy in a pile of paper."

The boy didn't answer right away. When he spoke, his voice — the real voice, without the tube — was hoarse from little use, and smaller than Wren expected.

"Please," he said. "Don't tell anyone."

And the paper dragon, up close, no longer looked frightening. It looked like what it was: the loneliest thing Wren had ever seen in her life.

chapters.title: What Held the Fear Up
chapters.body:
His name was Alderic, and his story was sadder than any dragon.

Sitting on the cave floor, surrounded by gold no one had ever used, he told it. A hundred years ago, he said — because he was not the first; he had been trained by another, who had been trained by another before — a boy of Highwall, clever and scared and alone, had built the first paper dragon. The town was at war with the neighboring villages, and the boy discovered that if the town believed a terrible beast protected it from the mountain, the enemies would be afraid to attack, and the townspeople themselves would stay united by their shared fear. It worked. The town stopped being attacked. And the boy, whom no one loved, secretly became the most important thing in the world: the keeper of the fear that kept everyone safe.

But a dragon needs a dragon. When that first boy grew old, he chose another — an orphan, someone no one would miss — and trained him, and passed the secret along. And so it went for a hundred years. The tribute of gold fed the false dragon. And the tribute of people… Alderic lowered his eyes as he told this part. The people given to the dragon were not eaten. They were recruited. Whenever the dragon who operated the machine grew old or fell ill, the lottery was arranged by the elders — who knew the secret, the few who knew — to choose someone expendable, someone who asked too many questions or whom no one would come looking for, to become the next dragon. The other tributes, when they wouldn't do, were kept away, or worse. Alderic wouldn't explain the worse.

"I was given up when I was ten," he said. "For asking too many questions, just like you. And for four years I've lived in here, alone, being a monster for a town that hates me without knowing I exist, keeping everyone safe from a danger that I am. " He laughed, and the laugh was worse than crying. "I'm the thing that protects everyone. And I'm the loneliest person in the world. Both at the same time."

Wren listened to all of it. And her fury, which had gone away with the shock, came back — but this time aimed at the right place. Not at the dragon. At the town that preferred a convenient monster to facing the truth. At the elders who sacrificed children and called it safety.

"That's horrible," she said. "You were locked up here to prop up a lie."

"It's a lie that works," said Alderic, repeating, you could tell, words that had been drilled into him. "Without the dragon, the town has no protection. The enemies come back. People turn on each other. The fear keeps everyone together and safe. That's what I was told. That's why I stay."

"And do you believe that?"

Alderic was quiet for a long time.

"I have to believe it," he said, quietly. "Otherwise the four years in here mean nothing."

And here it was, Wren understood, the real prison. It was not the cave walls. It was the idea that the lie was necessary. It was believing that being a lonely monster was the fair price of everyone's safety. Alderic could leave the cave at any moment — there were no bars. But he didn't leave, because he had been convinced that the world needed him right there, suffering, so it wouldn't collapse.

Wren stood up. She held out her hand to him.

"Come with me," she said.

"Where? I can't go back. I'm the dragon. If I appear, they'll kill me or put someone else in my place. And then the town finds out there was never any dragon, and—"

"And then the town will have to learn to live without fear," said Wren. "Which is what it should have done a hundred years ago." She kept her hand out. "Listen, Alderic. You spent four years believing you're only good for being a monster who scares everyone from far away. But I came here to die and you didn't eat me. You asked, please, for me not to tell. The first thing you did when you saw me wasn't to roar. It was to be afraid, just like me." Her voice grew softer. "A real monster wouldn't be afraid. You're not the dragon. You're just a boy who was left alone in the dark too long. And I'm not leaving you here."

Alderic looked at her hand. He looked at the dark interior of the paper dragon where he had lived for four years. He looked at the useless piled gold, at the bellows and the ropes and the tube that stole his voice and turned it into a roar.

"And if the town collapses without the dragon?" he whispered. "And if it's all my fault?"

"Then we deal with it together," said Wren. "But I'd rather have a town that learns to be brave than one that only stays together because it's afraid of the same lie. That's not safety, Alderic. It's just fear with a dragon's name." She wiggled her outstretched hand. "Come on. No one should have to be everyone's nightmare to feel important. You matter even without being a monster. Let me show you."

And Alderic — who for four years had not heard anyone say his name with kindness, who for four years had been a roar and a smoke and never a boy — took her hand.

The two of them walked out of the cave together, into the dawn light that Alderic had not seen properly in far too long. Behind them, the paper dragon stayed behind, hollow and still and false, rustling faintly in the wind that came in through the mouth of the cave.

What happened to Highwall afterward is a longer story, and a harder one, and it doesn't fit here whole. There was shouting. There were elders unmasked. There were days of panic when the town, without its dragon, was afraid of everything — of attacks that never came, of neighbors who, in the end, were also tired of war. And there was, slowly, an astonishing discovery: that without the dragon to unite them through fear, people had to learn to unite through something else. It was harder. It was slower. But it was real.

As for Wren and Alderic, they walked together for many years, and each was, for the other, living proof of something they had both learned in cave and square: that fear is the most convincing liar in the world, and that courage is almost never about slaying the dragon. Most of the time, it's about getting close enough to see that the dragon is as scared as you are — and holding out your hand anyway.
